name: Lake Malawi National Park
blurb: Rock-dwelling cichlids, plankton and fish eagles at the southern end of the lake.

tip.title: Thin out the mbuna
tip.text: Mbuna graze algae on the rocks and feed the predatory haps, kingfishers, monitors and fish eagles. Set Mbuna to -100% and watch what happens next.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Tropical sunshine drives algae growth in the clear shallows and on the rocks of the lake edge.
Rain feeds the lake and wets the lakeshore woodland, helping trees such as baobab and fig grow.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead algae, plants and animals, returning nutrients to the water and soil.
Tiny floating algae that form the base of the open-water food chain in the lake.

nodes.name: Rock algae (aufwuchs)
nodes.desc: A film of algae and small organisms growing on rocks, grazed by rock-dwelling cichlids.
A huge, long-lived tree of the dry woodland around the lake. It is recorded often near the park.
Small drifting animals such as copepods, cladocerans and ostracods that graze phytoplankton.

nodes.name: Chambo
nodes.desc: Tilapia that feed mainly on phytoplankton. They are an important food fish for people and wildlife.
A common, widespread songbird that eats fruit such as figs.
Hovers over open water, then plunges to catch fish. It also takes crustaceans and large aquatic insects.
A generalist predator and scavenger eating fish, eggs, carrion, frogs, insects, birds and small mammals.
Fish are its main prey, snatched from a perch with its talons. It is the most-recorded bird of the area.
An ambush predator that mostly eats fish, but also takes land animals at the water edge, and scavenges.
A secretive big cat of the park. Baboons are a regular prey for leopards across southern Africa.
